detail.abstract:
The world’s richest man says money is ending. For years he has described money as “a series of heterogeneous databases insecurely connected with high latency” whose “primary purpose” is the allocation of human time; more recently he has said that “energy is the true currency,” that money “might be measured in terms of wattage,” and that “mass & energy will take the place of dollars.” His companies now report to the SEC in metric tons to orbit and gigawatts of compute, hold some thirty thousand bitcoin between them, and operate a segment called Super Intelligence. This Article takes him at his word. It reconstructs his monetary theory from the primary record, separates what he has said from what his firms have done, and places both in two histories: the energy-money movements of the 1930s, Technocracy and Social Credit, in each of which his grandfather was a leader; and the long debate over whether money can be abolished, replaced by a physical unit, or computed away. The Article argues that Musk’s “end of money” is best understood as a proposal about measure: that claims on output be denominated not in a legal unit, a liability of a sovereign, but in physical units, which are liabilities of no one and are therefore administered by whoever owns the physical stack. That proposal is the oldest heresy in monetary thought, and it fails as it always has. Money is not a measurement of a quantity; it is a legal institution for creating, ranking, and discharging claims, and the unit in which claims are written is a constitutional choice. Superintelligence will not end money. It will end the wage as the principal channel of claims on the product, multiply money among machines, and retire the computational argument against planning while leaving the political one standing. Monetary theory concedes the premise, money is memory, and refuses the conclusion, memory needs a keeper; the proposed transition, a dividend in a unit the state no longer taxes, releases the dollar rather than using it. The question left is who keeps the ledger, in what unit, and under what law. It closes with a program, a public law of calculation, and with the wrinkle that the law in question is now partly machine output.

title: Re-examining Schumpeter’s Legacy: Creative Destruction as Competition, Innovation and Capitalism

detail.title: Re-examining Schumpeter’s Legacy: Creative Destruction as Competition, Innovation and Capitalism

affiliations.org_name: École Normale Supérieure (ENS)
affiliations.preferred_name: École Normale Supérieure (ENS)

detail.abstract: This article argues that the predominant interpretations of Schumpeter in competition law and economics are inaccurate. The aim of the article is to qualify some of the ossified narratives around Schumpeter’s legacy. To identify these misinterpretations, the article first provides an overview of the concept of creative destruction and Schumpeter’s account of ‘monopolistic practices’ as they were developed in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy, Schumpeter’s most famous work to date (Section 2). It then lays out the prevalent competition law and economics accounts of Schumpeter (Section 3). This section focuses on the so-called ‘Schumpeterian thesis’, i.e., the proposition that big business or monopoly is more advantageous to innovation, which is attributed to Schumpeter. It shows how the so-called Schumpeterian thesis is connected to Schumpeter’s creative destruction in the literature. It also surveys various ‘Schumpeterian’ proposals of antitrust analysis built on creative destruction. The following Section 4 sets out the misinterpretations surrounding Schumpeter by contrasting the previous two sections, and by laying out Schumpeter’s thinking and scholarship in general. It details Schumpeter’s views on the concepts of monopoly and perfect competition, on the economic theories and policies of his day, his vision of the entrepreneur as the force behind creative destruction and his theory of entrepreneurial decline – all almost entirely missing from the popular works on Schumpeter in competition law and economics. Section 5 concludes.

title: The World Peace Framework (WPF): A Policy Architecture for Establishing Permanent Global Peace through Universal Deterrence

detail.title: The World Peace Framework (WPF): A Policy Architecture for Establishing Permanent Global Peace through Universal Deterrence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or non-financial competing interests to report regarding this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve human subjects, animal testing, or unpublished clinical patient data; therefore, formal ethics approval was not required for this study.

affiliations.org_name: Independent Policy Researcher
affiliations.preferred_name: Independent Policy Researcher

detail.abstract: War persists not because most states want it, but because the structure of the international system makes it rational. In the absence of an authority capable of reliably protecting states from one another, uncertainty over rivals' intentions and the continued high payoff of aggression mean that states often arm out of fear and attack out of greed, even when mutual restraint is the better outcome for all. This paper proposes the World Peace Framework (WPF), a policy framework designed to address that gap: an attack against one is an attack against all, encompassing every community, every state, and humanity as a whole. Built upon the design requirements of universality, mutuality, credibility, pragmatism and robustness, the WPF is grounded in the moral position that human lives matter most, while aggression must not be rewarded, because a world where conquest pays is a world in which more lives are lost. The purpose of the WPF is to remove the payoff of aggression entirely by increasing deterrence to the point where the costs of aggression outweigh any potential gains, making restraint the only rational decision for a state. This means if a state commits an armed attack across a protected control line, a predetermined sequence of verification and attribution, coordinated economic measures and a collective global military response aim to reverse that violation. Military operations freeze once the protected line is restored and a ceasefire is verified, while the underlying territorial dispute remains subject to diplomatic and legal resolution. Adopted by a two-thirds vote with no veto, stress-tested across multiple scenarios, evaluated for its peace dividend, and supported by defined conflict-resolution mechanisms and a clear implementation roadmap establishing the governance model, the WPF seeks to transform international security from selective deterrence into universal protection, making world peace a structural feature of the international order.

detail.abstract: We use LLMs as synthetic survey respondents to elicit green tastes, return beliefs, portfolio allocations, and investment motives from 480 retail and 60 institutional investor identities. Compared with retail, institutions report weaker tastes yet greener portfolio tilts, citing outside pressure. A greener tilt therefore need not indicate a stronger taste for greenness.  Retail tastes depend mostly on political affiliation, institutional tastes on type and geography.  Beliefs differ across the three ESG dimensions, with high-governance portfolios expected to outperform. We reconstruct survey responses under 2014--2025 information environments using date-masked information modules shuffled across years. Tastes vary little over time, but beliefs about green portfolios become more pessimistic after 2020. The two reconstructed series relate to different real-world data: tastes to measures of green demand, beliefs to measures of attention.

title: Meta's $17.1 Billion Jawboned Settlement and the First Amendment Challenges Ahead
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago School of Law

detail.title: Meta's $17.1 Billion Jawboned Settlement and the First Amendment Challenges Ahead

affiliations.org_name: University of Illinois Chicago School of Law
affiliations.preferred_name: University of Illinois Chicago School of Law

detail.abstract:
Beginning in 2024, state legislatures began passing laws as part of an effort to regulate access to social media platforms for young users.  By 2026, at least 12 states had passed statutes requiring age-verification of social media users and setting limits on access for youth users.  All of these laws have already been challenged in court, and several have been preliminarily or permanently enjoined because courts found that they violate the First Amendment rights of platform users.

 In August 2026, Meta settled claims brought by 52 states and territories that its platforms--Facebook and Instagram--were negligently designed and caused harm to young users. As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to implement mandatory age-authentication for all platform users. This short article argues that this settlement is a new form of Jawboning--an action by the government to restrict speech by pressuring an intermediary to impose restrictions on third parties.  The article discusses Supreme Court precedent in this area and puts forward alternative ways that states could make young users safer online without restricting speech in these important forums.

detail.abstract:
“Superintelligence” is now a line on an income statement. In October 2026 the company that owns the rockets, the satellites, the social network, the chatbot, and the payment app reported $7.6 billion of quarterly revenue from a segment it calls Super Intelligence, and its controller disclosed that it and its sister company, which builds the cars, the batteries, and the humanoid robots, had each formed a special committee to consider merging. SpaceX alone expects, by the end of 2027, to be running at between $500 billion and $1 trillion of annual recurring revenue. The controller (Elon Musk) holds 82 percent of the votes in one, is working toward a quarter in the other, and has said, for a decade, what the enterprise will do to money, to work, and to the state. This Article takes those statements as a program, sourced firsthand and read against the documents in which the firm speaks under liability, and treats “X” as a placeholder for the whole: the everything app and the everything firm. Its claim is that the firm’s political economy rests on an asymmetry. The firm’s claims on the public are fixed in law: supervoting shares, awards that vest on a $7.5 trillion market capitalization, a million-person colony on Mars, and a hundred terawatts of compute in orbit, a three-percent threshold for derivative suits, mandatory arbitration, and terms of service capped at one hundred dollars of liability. The public’s claims on the firm are promises of earning, made, deferred, restructured, and withdrawn at the firm’s discretion for ten years: that a car would earn its owner thirty thousand dollars a year, that creators would “make a living,” that there would be jobs on Mars, and that the state will send everyone a check because the firm’s robots will make inflation impossible. The Article names this arrangement, traces its kin in the company-state, the company town, and the energy-certificate schemes, compares the regulatory postures forming toward it in the United States, the European Union, Switzerland, and the Gulf, and projects its arc across the decade of the controller’s vesting schedule, in three phases and three scenarios. It closes with a program, old in principle: earnings paid in the coin of the realm, on published terms, with a right of exit; and a state that decides what it will tax before it becomes the firm’s paymaster of last resort.

title: Scale and Scope in the Value of Data

detail.title: Scale and Scope in the Value of Data

affiliations.org_name: University of Toulouse 1 - Department of Economics
affiliations.preferred_name: Toulouse School of Economics

detail.abstract: Claims of diminishing returns to data measure data by volume. I model data as three inputs: observations, their attributes, and those a firm predicts with. In high dimensions, a learning multiplier links the attributes: with each attribute it trains on, the firm learns the others' effects better, so returns to attributes can increase. The multiplier, a sufficient statistic for these spillovers, can be measured by estimating a learning curve. Learning precision grows more than proportionally with observations, and returns to them can increase, provided that the firm trains on attributes stronger than some it predicts with and samples are small.

detail.abstract: Albrecht and Hovenkamp present a clear and precise defense of the Consumer Welfare Standard ("CWS") which takes head on the criticisms leveled by Mark Glick, Gabriel Lozada and Darren Bush. They contend that the economic criticism leveled by the welfare economists on both consumer surplus and the Kaldor and Hicks New Welfare Economics approach to measuring welfare do not pose practical challenges for CWS when applied to single antitrust markets. They claim that consumer surplus is capable of aggregating several competitive goals for antitrust. We challenge these conclusions by showing that the welfare economics critique renders the CWS an unreliable approach for antitrust analysis. We instead advocate that the CWS be replaced by the Protect Competition Standard, which is a simple way of once again enforcing antitrust regulations in a way that respects the traditional multiple Congressional goals for antitrust enforcement.

title: Oral Versus Injectable Incretin Therapy In Type 2 Diabetes: An Estimand-Harmonised Network Meta-Analysis Integrating The First Oral-Versus-Oral Head-To-Head Trial

detail.title: Oral Versus Injectable Incretin Therapy In Type 2 Diabetes: An Estimand-Harmonised Network Meta-Analysis Integrating The First Oral-Versus-Oral Head-To-Head Trial

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests

affiliations.org_name: Peking University
affiliations.preferred_name: Peking University

detail.abstract:
Background: Orforglipron, a once-daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist taken without fasting restrictions, has completed phase 3 evaluation, including ACHIEVE-3, the first oral-versus-oral head-to-head trial. Existing network meta-analyses predate it and mix estimands, leaving the oral agents' standing unsettled. ¹˒²

Methods: In this network meta-analysis of phase 3 trials in type 2 diabetes, we compared orforglipron 36 mg, oral semaglutide 14 mg, subcutaneous semaglutide 1·0 mg, tirzepatide 15 mg, and dulaglutide 1·5 mg under one estimand the treatment-regimen (treatment-policy) estimand using ClinicalTrials.gov structured results cross-checked against trial reports. Co-primary endpoints were change in HbA1c and bodyweight at the primary endpoint (26–52 weeks). We fitted contrast-based random-effects network meta-analysis (Paule–Mandel τ²) with node-splitting and P-scores. A phase 2 retatrutide trial entered a sensitivity network only.

Findings: Seven trials (6,679 participants) formed the network. Tirzepatide ranked first for HbA1c (−2·13 points vs placebo, 95% CI −2·48 to −1·78), followed by subcutaneous semaglutide (−1·54) and orforglipron (−1·51), which were indistinguishable (−0·03, −0·52 to 0·46); then dulaglutide (−1·05) and oral semaglutide (−0·94). The orforglipron–oral semaglutide loop was inconsistent: direct ACHIEVE-3 evidence (−0·71) favoured orforglipron significantly more than the placebo-anchored indirect estimate (−0·20; node-split p=0·012). Bodyweight was consistent: tirzepatide (−9·45 kg) > orforglipron (−6·11) > subcutaneous semaglutide (−3·47) > dulaglutide (−2·72) > oral semaglutide (−2·26). Phase 2 retatrutide showed the largest weight effect (−13·91 kg).

Interpretation: On harmonised estimands, orforglipron matches weekly subcutaneous semaglutide on glycaemia and beats it on weight. But its advantage over oral semaglutide is 0·71 HbA1c points head-to-head versus 0·20 through placebo plausibly explained by duration, baseline HbA1c, and open-label dosing conditions. League tables ignoring this inconsistency overstate what is known.

detail.abstract:
Background: Hepatitis A incidence has declined substantially in China, but how disease risk is restructured across age, socioeconomic inequality, and spatial clustering during the transition from high to low endemicity remains poorly characterized.

Methods: In this serial cross-sectional study, national notifiable disease surveillance data from 31 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities of mainland China (January 1990 to December 2023; 1990–2004 data from the national epidemic data compendium) were analyzed. Trends were estimated using joinpoint (segmented) regression with a negative binomial model; seasonality, age-specific trends, Human Development Index (HDI)-related inequality (slope index of inequality [SII] and concentration index [CI]), and spatial clustering (Moran’s I, local indicators of spatial association, Getis-Ord Gi*) were assessed.

Findings: 4,928,677 hepatitis A cases were reported between 1990 and 2023; incidence declined from 52.48 to 0.82 per 100,000 population (98.4% decrease), with joinpoints in June 1996, July 2008, and February 2010 and the steepest decline after July 2008 (annual percentage change −26.27%). Seasonality persisted (peak in August, +11.78%; trough in February, −18.88%). The case share of persons aged ≥60 years increased from 2.08% to 35.84% (p<0.001), and declines weakened with age (−17.26% per year at ages 5–9 years vs −2.02% at ages 80–84 years). Inequality reversed: the SII changed from +20.77 in 1990 to −0.345 in 2022 and the CI from +0.064 to −0.049. Global spatial autocorrelation peaked in 2012 (Moran’s I 0.669) and became nonsignificant after 2020, whereas high–high clustering persisted in western provinces and re-emerged in Sichuan and Tibet in 2023.

Interpretation: Hepatitis A incidence declined substantially, but remaining risk is concentrated among older, insufficiently vaccinated adults and lower-HDI western regions. Sustaining childhood immunization, extending vaccination to adults, and strengthening hotspot surveillance may constitute a generalizable framework for control in the low-endemicity phase.
